In this report soft emissions of photons and gluons are studied from a hard photon decay to a particle/antiparticle pair. Included is the derivation of the matrix elements for such processes with focus on the correlated emission of gluons and the application of the collinear limit. The resulting angular ordering is studied as is the comparison of gluon emissions to photon emissions and the running of the strong coupling constant.

\section{Introduction}
In the decay of a Z boson or photon into a quark/antiquark pair it is possible for gluons to then be emitted from the quarks, a process that contributes to hadronization and jet structure. In the limit where these gluons are soft and collinear the matrix elements for these interactions simplify in an interesting way.\\
\linebreak
In this report we will consider the decay of a photon first into an electron-positron pair when we look at the simpler case of photon emissions. Then we shall look at the decay into a quark-antiquark pair from which gluon emissions will be studied.\\
The decays will be of the form in fig 1.1 but for brevity we shall re-write the diagram in the 'decay product form' in fig 1.2

\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{decay}
\caption{The decay diagram, the products are $e^-e^+$ in section 2 and $q\bar{q}$ in section 3  }
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[h!]

\includegraphics[width=0.4\textwidth]{productform}
\caption{The decay product form}
\end{figure}
\subsection{Assumptions}

Throughout this report certain assumptions will be used that greatly simplify the calculations and enable us to produce much simpler expressions for the matrix elements.These are: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Softness of the emitted gluons with respect to the quarks. This means that for gluon 4-momentum k and quark/antiquark 4-momenta $P_1, P_2$; $k<<P_1,P_2$ and we can neglect any terms quadratic in k.
\item Massless quarks. The momenta involved in the interaction are such that the masses are negligible and can be neglected. This assumption also allows us to simplify our calculations further by using the dirac equations $\bar{u}(p_1)\not{p_1}=0, \not{p_2}v(p_2)=0$
\item Collinearity. The gluon momenta are at small angles from the quark momenta. The decay products are at small angles to each other.   
\end{enumerate}
   
\section{Comparison with QED}

In the photon decay to lepton/antilepton pair we can see radiative corrections with photons being emitted from the leptons. This situation is very similar to our gluon diagrams with some important differences. Since QCD is a non-abelian gauge theory the gluons have colour charge and can couple to other gluons; photons being chargeless cannot couple to other photons and so all photon emissons are \emph{independent} whereas we can have \emph{correlated} gluon emissions (where we have triple or higher gluon verticies in our diagram).
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{ptoe}
\caption{Photon decay to electron-positron pair with no emission}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{electronnophoton}
\caption{In decay product form}
\end{figure}

The $ \gamma \rightarrow q \bar{q}$ decay with no photon emission shown in fig 2.1 is:
\begin{align}
M_{e^+e^-}=\epsilon_\mu (q) \bar{u}(p_1)ie\gamma^\mu v(p_2)
\end{align}
Where the momenta satisfy $q=p_1+p_2$. Henceforth the parent particle will have momentum $q$, the daughter fermions $p_1,p_2$ and any bosons will have $k_i$.

\subsection{One Photon Emission}
With one soft photon emission $\gamma \rightarrow q \bar{q}+\gamma$ we have two diagrams. From assumption (2) we have neglected the masses in the propagators. The diagrams for this decay follow the form in fig 2.3
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{electrononephoton}
\caption{The diagram for one photon emission}
\end{figure}
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma}=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie\gamma^\mu\left[ -i\frac{\not{p_2}+\not{k}}{(p_2+k)^2}\epsilon_\nu (k) ie\gamma^\nu + \epsilon_\nu (k) ie\gamma^\nu i\frac{\not{p_1}+\not{k}}{(p_1+k)^2}\right]v(p_2)
\end{align*} 
When we apply assumption (1) such that $(p_2+k)^2=p_2^2+k^2+2p_2.k=2p_2.k$ and the general expression $\not{p}\not{k}+\not{k}\not{p}=2p.k$ and remembering that $\epsilon_\mu \gamma^\mu=\not{\epsilon}$ and finally using the Dirac equations specified in assumption (2) we can then find:
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma}=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie^2 \gamma^\mu v(p_2)\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]
\end{align*}
and when we compare with (eq 2.1) we can then write:
\begin{equation}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma}=M_{e^+e^-}e\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]
\end{equation}
\begin{align*}
\vert M_{e^+e^-\gamma}\vert^2 &=e^2\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \sum\limits_{i} \epsilon_\mu^i \epsilon_\nu^{* i} \left[\frac{p_1^\mu}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2^\mu}{p_2.k}\right]\left[\frac{p_1^\nu}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2^\nu}{p_2.k}\right]\\
&=e^2\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}
\end{align*}
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{e^+e^-\gamma}\vert^2=e^2\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}
\end{equation}
Where we have used the sum over photon polarizations $\sum\limits_{i} \epsilon_\mu^i \epsilon_\nu^{* i}=-g_{\mu \nu}$ and we neglect terms like $p_1.p_1 or p_2.p_2$.

\subsection{Two Photon Emission}

Two photon emission proceeds in the say way as with one photon. We have 4 possible diagrams this time and so four terms in the amplitude. The momenta in this case satisfy $q=p_1+p_2+k_a+k_b$ with $k_a,k_b<<p_1,p_2$. In the two photon emission the \emph{softer photon is always emitted second}, as it cannot be emitted from a more off-shell line. This also holds true for gluons and shall be used later.
The first diagram component to the amplitude is:
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{electrontwophoton1}
\caption{Two photon emission from the decay products}
\end{figure} 
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma} &=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\nu \epsilon_\nu(k_a) i\frac{(\not{p_1}+\not{k_a})}{(p_1+k_a)^2} ie\gamma^\mu(-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_b)^2} ie\gamma^\rho \epsilon_\rho(k_b)v(p_2)\\
&=-\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
For the second diagram we can simply do $p_1 \Leftrightarrow p_2$ so that we get
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}=-\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
For the other two diagrams:
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{electrontwophoton2}
\caption{The diagram for the matrix element below}
\end{figure}
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}&=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu (-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_a+k_b)^2} ie\gamma^\nu \epsilon_\nu(k_a) (-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_b)^2} ie\gamma^\rho \epsilon_\rho(k_b)v(p_2)\\
&=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
And again reversing the quark momenta
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
Collecting all these together we get
\begin{align}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}&=M_{e^+e^-}e^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}+\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}\right]\\
&=M_{e^+e^-}e^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\right]\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}\right]
\end{align}
When we square this with the methods used to obtain eq.(2.3) we arrive at
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{e^+e^-\gamma}\vert^2=e^4\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_a p_2.k_a}\frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_b p_2.k_b}
\end{equation}
As we can see in eq(2.4) the number of terms in the matrix element is just the number of possible diagrams and the terms themselves are products of n factors like $\frac{p.\epsilon}{p.k}$ for n photons emitted. When we square the matrix element we find that for n emitted photons the squared matrix element is always of the form:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{e^+e^- n\gamma}\vert^2=\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \prod\limits_{i}^n W_i
\end{equation}
Where I define the W as
\begin{equation}
W_1:=g^2\frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_i p_2.k_i}
\end{equation}  
Expression (2.7) will reappear when we look at gluon emissions.  
\subsection{Coherence}
We now apply the collinearity assumption. This is that the the decay products (in the case of QED above it is an electron/positron pair)are at small angles and the emitted bosons are also at small angles.\\
\linebreak
In the QED matrix element we have the  W factor defined in eg(2.8) and if we remember that $p.k=E_p E_k-E_p E_k cos\theta_{pk}$. Since in this limit and using natural units we write $E=p$. This then implies that for the W factor we get.
\begin{align}
g^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}=\frac{g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{2(1-cos \theta_{12})}{(1-cos \theta_{1k})(1-cos \theta_{2k})}
\end{align}
Since also $E_k= \omega_k$ in natural units. The angle $\theta_{12}$ is the angle between the two fermions, $\theta_{1k}$ is the angle between fermion 1 and the photon k. This notation shall be used fro the rest of this document with the fermions as numbers and the bosons as latin letters. \\
As we are using the collinear assumption we also can replace the cosine with the first couple of terms in its taylor series and so eq (2.9) then becomes:
\begin{align}
\frac{g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{2(1-cos \theta_{12})}{(1-cos \theta_{1k})(1-cos \theta_{2k})}\simeq \frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{\theta_{12}^2}{\theta_{1k}^2 \theta_{2k}^2}
\end{align}
Here we now have two cases, one where $\theta_{1k} or  \theta_{2k}<<\theta_{12}$ i.e the boson is close in angle to one of the fermions in which case the expression above simplifies slightly, or we have $\theta_{12}<<\theta_{1k}\simeq \theta_{2k}$ where the emitted boson is far away in angle. This latter case is \emph{coherence} and the photon radiation is suppressed as we do not see the charges of the fermion pair. This means that the former case is of importance to us but not the latter. So we can now write eq (2.10) as a sum of the two cases where the boson is emitted close to one or the other using a step function $\Theta$.
\begin{equation}
\frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{\theta_{12}^2}{\theta_{1k}^2 \theta_{2k}^2}\simeq \frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{1}{\theta_{1k}^2} \Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{1k})+\frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{1}{\theta_{2k}^2} \Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{2k})
\end{equation}
This is angular ordering and shall be applied to QCD in section 4.
\section{QCD}
\subsection{One Gluon Emission}
One gluon emission proceeds like that of the one photon emission, since with only one boson we don't get any correlated emission. Differences however arise from the gluon vertex factor and the Gell-Mann matrix it contains. We consider the decay $\gamma\rightarrow q \bar{q}+g$. With diagrams of the form in fig 3.1.
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{onegluon}
\caption{Decay to quark antiquark pair with one gluon emission}
\end{figure}
So in this case the matrix element is 
\begin{align}
M_{q\bar{q}g}&=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie g_s \gamma^\mu v(p_2)t^a\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]\\
&=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s t^a\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]
\end{align}  
When we square the element we must use the sum $\sum\limits_a t^a t^a=C_f=4/3$
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}g}\vert^2=C_fg_s^2\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}
\end{equation}
We can see that this differs from the QED case only by the constants $e^2\Rightarrow C_f g_s^2$
\subsection{Two Gluon Emission}
For two gluon emission we have six diagrams and the prospect of correlated emission. This effect leads to the matrix element for the gluon case changing drastically from the much simpler two photon emission in eq(2.5).\\
\linebreak
Four of our six diagrams are independent emission diagrams and so are the same as the four diagrams of the two photon emission with the addition of Gell-Mann matrices from the quark-gluon vertex. So without the correlated emission our matrix element is:
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{twogluon1}
\caption{An independent emission of two gluons}
\end{figure}
\begin{equation}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s^2\left[t^bt^a\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}+t^at^b\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-t^at^b\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-t^bt^a\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}\right]
\end{equation}
\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{twogluon2}
\caption{On of the two correlated emission diagrams}
\end{figure}
The last two matrix elements come from the correlated emission of two gluons where we have a triple gluon vertex.
\begin{align*}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=\epsilon_\mu(q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie\gamma^\mu (-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_a+k_b)^2} i g_s\gamma^\nu t^d\frac{(-ig_{\nu\rho}\delta^{dc})}{(k_a+k_b)^2}(-1)g_s f^{abc}\\\left[g^{\rho\beta}(2k_a+k_b)^\gamma +g^{\beta\gamma}(-k_a+k_b)^\rho +g^{\gamma\rho} (-2k_b-k_a)^\beta \right]\epsilon_\beta^*(k_a) \epsilon_\gamma^* (k_b)v(p_2)
\end{align*}
We apply the 'second gluon is softer' condition so that we can ignore $k_b$ in the propagator and applying the other assumptions we get
\begin{align*}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}&=M_{q\bar{q}} i f^{abc}g_s^2 t^c \frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a})}{2p_2.k_a}\frac{\gamma^\nu g_{\nu\rho}}{2k_a.k_b}\\
&\left[\epsilon^{\rho*}(k_a)\epsilon_\gamma^* (k_b)(2k_a+k_b)^\gamma +\epsilon_a.\epsilon_b(-k_a+k_b)^\rho +\epsilon_\beta^*(k_a) \epsilon^{\rho*} (k_b)(-2k_b-k_a)^\beta \right]\\
&=M_{q\bar{q}} i f^{abc}g_s^2 t^c \frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a})}{2p_2.k_a}\frac{1}{2k_a.k_b}\left[\not{\epsilon_a}\epsilon_\gamma^* (k_b)(2k_a+k_b)^\gamma +\not{\epsilon_b}\epsilon_\beta^*(k_a)(-2k_b-k_a)^\beta \right]\\
&=M_{q\bar{q}} i f^{abc}g_s^2 t^c \frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{k_a.\epsilon_b}{k_a.k_b}
\end{align*}
We have ignored the term involving $\epsilon_a.\epsilon_b$ since it becomes like $\not{k}$ which we have neglected. The last component to the matrix element is found by the substitution $p_1\Leftrightarrow p_2$ into the equation above.\\
\linebreak
When we include all the components we find the total matrix element is 
\begin{equation}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\right]\left[t^bt^a \frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}-t^a t^b\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-i f^{abc}t^c \frac{k_a.\epsilon_b}{k_a.k_b} \right]
\end{equation}
To square the element we must sum over the different colour states of the gluons
\begin{align*}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2&=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_a p_2.k_a}[\sum\limits_{col}\frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_b p_2.k_b}t^a t^b t^a t^b +\\
&\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b} i f^{abc} (t^c t^b t^a-t^a t^b t^c)-\frac{p_1.k_a}{p_1.k_b k_a.k_b}if^{abc} (t^c t^a t^b - t^b t^a t^c)]\\
&=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2[\frac{W_a}{N_c} 2 W_b Tr(t^a t^b t^a t^b)+\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b} i f^{abc} Tr(t^c t^b t^a-t^a t^b t^c)\\
&-\frac{p_1.k_a}{p_1.k_b k_a.k_b}if^{abc} Tr(t^c t^a t^b - t^b t^a t^c)]
\end{align*}
I have used the W defined in eq(2.8)and now we can use some relations to simplify this result
\begin{align*}
t^a t^b t^a&=-\frac{t^b}{2N_c}\Rightarrow Tr(t^a t^b t^a t^b)=-\frac{Tr(t^b t^b)}{2N_c}=-C_f/2\\
&[t^a,t^b]=i f^{abc} t^c\Rightarrow i f^{abc} Tr(t^c t^b t^a-t^a t^b t^c)=f^{abc}f^{abd} Tr(t^c t^d)=C_a Tr(t^c t^c)=C_a^2 C_f
\end{align*}
$C_a=N_c$ and the above can simplify the squared amplitude to
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2  W_a C_f \left[N_c\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b}+N_c \frac{p_1.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_1.k_b}- \frac{1}{N_c}W_b\right]
\end{equation} 
\section{Angular Ordering}
We now wish to apply the result of the collinear limit outlined in section 2.3 onto our gluon emissions. The one gluon emission follows a very similar form to that of eq(2.11) except that it has the factor $C_f$. We shall proceed by first considering the two gluon emission squared matrix element in eq(3.6) but the first part will be absorbed into a one gluon matrix element:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2=g_s^2\vert M_{q\bar{q}g}\vert^2 \left[N_c\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b}+N_c \frac{p_1.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_1.k_b}- \frac{1}{N_c}W_b\right]
\end{equation}
Now using the same method in eq(2.9)and eq(2.10) the three factors in the brackets are rewritten to become:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2\simeq g_s^2\vert M_{q\bar{q}g}\vert^2 \frac{N_c}{\omega^2_b}\left[\frac{2 \theta^2_{2a}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{2b}} +\frac{2\theta^2_{1a}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{1b}}-\frac{1}{4 N_c^2}\frac{\theta^2_{12}}{\theta^2_{1b}\theta^2_{2b}}\right]
\end{equation}
If we include the first gluon contribution we get:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2\simeq g_s^4 C_f \vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \frac{4}{\omega^2_a}\frac{N_c}{\omega^2_b}\frac{\theta^2_{12}}{\theta^2_{1a}\theta^2_{2a}} \left[\frac{2 \theta^2_{2a}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{2b}} +\frac{2\theta^2_{1a}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{1b}}-\frac{1}{4 N_c^2}\frac{\theta^2_{12}}{\theta^2_{1b}\theta^2_{2b}}\right]
\end{equation}
We now consider the different ordering cases. There are eight cases for two gluon emission. We first expect the single gluon part (inside$\vert M_{q\bar{q}g}\vert^2$) to undergo the ordering procedure like the photon in eq(2.11). This means that we can write:
\begin{align}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2\simeq g_s^4 C_f \vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \frac{N_c}{\omega^2_b}\frac{4}{\omega^2_a}\left[\frac{1}{\theta_{1a}^2} \Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{1a})+\frac{1}{\theta_{2a}^2} \Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{2a})\right]\left[\frac{2 \theta^2_{2a}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{2b}} +\frac{2\theta^2_{1a}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{1b}}-\frac{1}{4 N_c^2}\frac{\theta^2_{12}}{\theta^2_{1b}\theta^2_{2b}}\right]
\end{align}
The part of the squared amplitude that corresponds to the second gluon undergoes the process in a more complicated manner since it has three terms whereas we only needed to consider one term in eq(2.11).\\
\linebreak
For the first gluon above and for the photons in eq (2.11) we made the assumption that the angle the photon/gluon makes with one fermion is much smaller than the other and so we can use the step function of the form in the first part in eq(4.4). When we try to apply the same constraint to the second gluon part it does not easily reduce in the same way.\\
\linebreak
We might expect that each of the three terms in the last factor of eq(4.4) would produce two step function terms as it has done for the single gluon factor that precedes it.   
\section{N Gluon Emission}
We have seen that in both QED and QCD for a matrix element of  n diagrams (possible emission pathways) describing m independent emissions we have a sum of n products of m factors like $\frac{p.\epsilon}{p.k}$ when we include diagrams with correlated emission in QCD we will get terms like $if^{abc}\frac{k.\epsilon}{k.k}$ for each triple gluon vertex in our diagram.\\
\linebreak
A general N-gluon result for the squared matrix element that shall I simply quote from the lectures of Salam is:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}ng}\vert^2\simeq\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \prod\limits^n_{i=1}\frac{4 g_s^2}{\omega^2_i}\frac{C_s \Theta(\omega_{i-1}-\omega_i)}{min(\theta_{qg},...,\theta_{gg})^2}
\end{equation}
However it can be seen that for a general N gluon squared amplitude there would be more than one term and this expression cannot produce a sum of terms that is required. For a two gluon emission this expression results in:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2\simeq\vert M_{q\bar{q}g}\vert^2 \frac{4g_s^2}{\omega_a^2}\frac{4g_s^2}{\omega_b^2}C^2_f\frac{\Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{k1})}{\theta_{k1}^2}\frac{\Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{k2})}{\theta_{k2}^2}
\end{equation}
Which is clearly very different from the result we have derived in the last section.

\section{The Running of the Strong Coupling}  
Does the correlated emission part of the two soft gluon matrix element look like a one gluon emission with a running coupling constant? We know that a triple gluon vertex in a diagram will always introduce a term like $if^{abc}t^c \frac{k.\epsilon}{k.k}$ into our matrix element. From the Gell-Mann matrix identity
\begin{equation}
\left[t^a,t^b\right]=if^{abc}t^c
\end{equation}
We can always write this term as two products of the same factors we have with independent emission, albeit with the gluon momenta rather than the quark momenta. This means we can re-write the element for two gluon emissions eq(3.5) as
\begin{equation}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\right]\left[t^bt^a \frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}-t^a t^b\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-t^a t^b\frac{k_a.\epsilon_b}{k_a.k_b}+t^b t^a \frac{k_a.\epsilon_b}{k_a.k_b} \right]
\end{equation} 
This looks like a matrix element of wholly independent emissions with a very soft gluon being emitted from the initial gluon line, which is what we expect.\\
\linebreak
If we consider a situation where the gluons acted like photons and didn't self-interact; they would have a squared matrix element like:
\begin{equation}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2_{alt}=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2  C_f^2 W_a W_b
\end{equation}
and if we divide our actual two gluon emission squared matrix element by this we will the effect of the non-abelian nature of QCD.
\begin{equation}
\frac{\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2}{\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2_{alt}}=\frac{N_c}{2 C_f}\left[\frac{p_2.k_a p_1 .k_b}{k_a .k_b p_1.p_2}+\frac{p_1.k_a p_2 .k_b}{k_a .k_b p_1.p_2}-\frac{1}{N_c^2}\right]
\end{equation} 
If we apply the collinear assumption and use the approximations of section 4 then this becomes:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2}{\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2_{alt}}=\frac{N_c}{2C_f}\left[\frac{\theta^2_{2a}\theta^2_{1c}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{12}}+\frac{\theta^2_{1a}\theta^2_{2b}}{\theta^2_{ab}\theta^2_{12}}-\frac{1}{N_c^2}\right]
\end{equation}
